step1_summary: Chief complaint: 5 days of cough and constantly streaming/runny nose

Symptoms: - Cough: dry, started ~5 days ago, occurs every 20–30 minutes, no sputum, no haemoptysis, no chest pain, no dyspnoea or pleuritic pain. - Nasal discharge: continuous, described as green. - Systemic: subjective fevers (hot to touch) with chills, myalgias/aching muscles. - GI: brief diarrhoea around onset (resolved). - Duration: ~5 days. - Aggravating/alleviating: lemon/lemsip soothes throat; resting otherwise; no other self treatments except lemsip.
Past medical history: Diabetes (type not specified), Hypertension
Medications/allergies: Reported on metformin and lisinopril (dose reported incorrectly as 'two hundred'); seasonal hay fever (allergic rhinitis) history; no known drug allergies
Family/social history: Lives with partner and a dog; works as an office manager; alcohol: 'the odd cherry' (unclear); smoking status not stated

Vital signs/exam findings: No measured temperature recorded; patient reports feeling hot and chilly at times; no objective vitals recorded; no respiratory distress on history; no focal chest exam findings documented

V: Pulmonary embolism: Rationale — can present with acute cough and dyspnoea but transcript lacks pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, haemoptysis or risk-factor history; low pretest probability here.
I: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold): Rationale — acute onset 5 days, runny nose, dry cough, myalgias, self-limited course and partial symptomatic improvement with simple remedies; most likely per doctor.
Acute bronchitis: Rationale — dry cough predominant, can follow URTI, cough frequent every 20–30 minutes; usually viral.
Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis: Rationale — green nasal discharge and persistent nasal symptoms; bacterial sinusitis considered if symptoms prolonged or severe.
COVID-19 / influenza: Rationale — cough, feverish feelings and myalgia could be viral including COVID/influenza; needs testing depending on local guidance.
N: Lung cancer (endobronchial tumour): Rationale — can cause persistent cough but unlikely with acute 5-day onset and lack of risk factors or systemic weight loss.
D: Post-viral cough (reactive airways) / bronchial hyperreactivity: Rationale — cough can persist after viral infection and be dry and frequent.
I2: ACE inhibitor (lisinopril) cough: Rationale — lisinopril commonly causes a chronic dry cough due to bradykinin accumulation; patient is on lisinopril and has a dry cough, though onset here is acute and recent.
Drug-related allergic reaction: Rationale — less likely; no new medications reported.
C: Chronic congenital airway anomaly: Rationale — unlikely to explain acute presentation in adult with previously no chronic chest problems.
A: Allergic rhinitis exacerbation: Rationale — patient has a history of hay fever; allergic rhinitis can cause rhinorrhoea and cough, but green discharge and systemic symptoms favour infection.
T: Inhalational/aspiration event: Rationale — could cause cough but no history of choking or aspiration reported.
E: Poorly controlled diabetes-related increased infection risk: Rationale — diabetes predisposes to more severe or bacterial infections; relevant as modifier rather than primary cause.
Thyrotoxicosis: Rationale — can cause heat intolerance and sweating but does not fit acute cough/runny nose presentation.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute 5-day history of runny nose, dry cough, myalgia and subjective feverish feelings with partial symptomatic relief from symptomatic measures is most consistent with a viral URTI; common and matches the clinician's impression.
supporting_evidence: Onset ~5 days with runny nose and dry cough
No shortness of breath, chest pain, haemoptysis or severe features
Partial improvement with symptomatic treatment (lemsip, lemon)
opposing_evidence: Green nasal discharge (often thought to suggest bacterial infection, though not specific)
Diabetes increases risk for bacterial infection (raises concern for complication)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Frequent dry cough every 20–30 minutes with preceding URTI symptoms fits acute bronchitis, usually viral and self-limited; absence of sputum, haemoptysis or systemic toxicity keeps bacterial bronchitis less likely.
supporting_evidence: Recent URTI-type nasal symptoms and myalgia
No focal chest pain or dyspnoea suggesting pneumonia
opposing_evidence: No auscultatory/physical exam recorded to confirm bronchitic findings
Short duration (5 days) — could still be early URTI rather than lower airway involvement

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Lisinopril is a known cause of a dry, persistent cough; patient is taking lisinopril and reports a dry cough. However, ACE inhibitor cough is typically chronic and develops after weeks–months rather than acutely within days, making this less likely as the sole cause here.
opposing_evidence: Onset clearly 5 days and temporally related to other URTI symptoms
Patient reports accompanying rhinorrhoea, feverish feelings and myalgias which point to infectious cause

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Green nasal discharge and persistent nasal symptoms raise possibility of bacterial sinusitis, especially if symptoms worsen or persist >10 days or are severe. At day 5 without severe features, bacterial cause is less likely but should be considered if not improving or if fever persists.
supporting_evidence: Green nasal discharge and persistent rhinorrhoea
Facial sinus symptoms were asked about though patient did not report focal sinus pain
opposing_evidence: Duration only ~5 days (bacterial sinusitis usually suspected at >10 days or if severe acute presentation)
No localized facial pain/pressure, no high measured fever recorded

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Viral syndromes such as COVID-19 or influenza can present with cough, feverish feelings and myalgias. Should be considered/testing guided by local prevalence and exposure, but no specific testing performed and symptoms so far not severe.
supporting_evidence: Cough, subjective fever and myalgias consistent with viral respiratory infections
opposing_evidence: No anosmia, no high measured fever documented, and no severe symptoms requiring immediate escalation
